solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Piece round prow's buckled strong spar

indicators.note: round says one piece goes all the way about the other, enclosing it
something buckled is bent out of shape, so these letters are pushed into a new order

parts.note: the possessive taken as plain letters

explanation.surface: A ship's battered prow has a piece fitted round it to support a heavy spar.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive's apostrophe is ignored, so prow's supplies five plain letters for the jumble.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowsprit is the stout pole projecting forward from a sailing ship's bow, carrying rigging for the foresails.

clue.text: Dislodge family avoiding clown

indicators.note: avoiding means leaving out, so one word is taken away from the other

parts.note: a bumpkin is a clumsy rustic, a clown in the old sense

explanation.surface: Someone tries to oust a family while steering clear of a clown.
explanation.walkthrough: Take KIN from BUMPKIN to leave BUMP.
explanation.definitionFit: To bump someone is to knock or push them out of their place, as when a passenger is bumped from a flight.

clue.text: Work with rubber, reverse of ideal, in Covent Garden stuff? (10, two words)

parts.note: op is short for opus, a work
a rubber is a pencil eraser

indicators.note: the reverse of something is it read the other way round, last letter first

parts.note: A1 means first-rate, ideal; the 1 serves as the letter I

explanation.surface: A puzzled request for some kind of work involving a rubber at the Royal Opera House.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 written backwards is 1A, read as IA. Covent Garden is the London home of the Royal Opera, so its 'stuff' is opera; the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: Opera seria is the serious, heroic Italian opera of the eighteenth century, the kind of work staged at the Royal Opera House.

clue.text: Deep-red apple from Spain we rushed, …

indicators.note: things rushed are done hastily and messily, so these letters come out jumbled

explanation.surface: We hurried off from Spain with a red apple, the ellipsis carrying the story into the next clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Winesap is an American apple variety with a dark red skin and a winy flavour.

clue.text: …in cheap wine stink, litre bottled

indicators.note: something bottled is shut up inside a container, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: ponk is slang for a bad smell
L is the symbol for litre

explanation.surface: Continuing from 3, a cheap wine that smells, with a litre of it bottled.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes inside PONK to give PLONK.
explanation.definitionFit: Plonk is informal British slang for cheap, ordinary wine of poor quality.

clue.text: China grass is leaning in cocked hat

parts.note: rami is an Asian nettle fibre also called China grass

explanation.surface: Some grass from China rests at an angle inside a cocked hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A Ramil(l)ies was an eighteenth-century three-cornered hat, named after Marlborough's victory at Ramillies.

clue.text: Bullrush in spa cut from flattened spoon

indicators.note: cut from means removed out of, so one word comes off the other

parts.note: a spatule is a spatula, a broad flat spoon-like tool

explanation.surface: A bulrush found at a spa is cut out with a flat spoon.
explanation.walkthrough: SPATULE without SPA leaves TULE.
explanation.definitionFit: Tule is a large bulrush of marshes in the western United States, the name coming from Nahuatl.

clue.text: Dry cask containing minimum of rosé

indicators.note: containing means holding inside, so one piece is placed within the other

parts.note: but is a variant spelling of butt, a large cask

indicators.note: the minimum of a word is its smallest part, a single opening letter

explanation.surface: A dry wine in a cask holding a little rosé.
explanation.walkthrough: R goes inside BUT, an old spelling of butt, to give BRUT.
explanation.definitionFit: Brut is the term for very dry champagne and sparkling wines, those with almost no added sugar.

clue.text: Mild cheese pales when grated busy fellow swallows (8, two words)

indicators.note: swallowing takes something inside, so one piece goes within the other
grating breaks a thing into shreds, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

explanation.surface: A mild cheese goes pale on being grated, and an industrious man gobbles it up.
explanation.walkthrough: The busy bee is a stock crossword fellow, and here he does the swallowing.
explanation.definitionFit: Bel Paese is a soft, creamy, mild Italian table cheese whose name means 'beautiful country'.

clue.text: Sun before night shortened beacon?

indicators.note: something shortened has lost its end, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: Ra is the Egyptian sun god

explanation.surface: The sun sets before a short night, with a beacon guiding someone.
explanation.walkthrough: DARK loses its K. The question mark shows the definition is loose: a radar beacon sends out signals to guide craft.
explanation.definitionFit: Radar is a system that locates objects by reflected radio waves, and radar beacons act as navigational markers for ships and aircraft.

clue.text: Such as Circe, inane and curt within similarly truncated

indicators.note: within means placed inside, so one piece sits in the other
truncated means cut short at the end, and similarly says the same cut applies to both words

explanation.surface: Sorceresses like Circe are described as foolish and rude in equally cut-down terms.
explanation.walkthrough: Similarly means both words lose the same thing, their last letter, before one goes inside the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Circe lured Odysseus's men to her island and turned them into swine, so she is an example of the seducers who entice.

clue.text: Entangle a quill mostly damaged and mostly corroded

indicators.note: the letters of a quill are largely knocked out of order, read as an instruction to rearrange them

parts.note: the six letters of these words are the fodder

indicators.note: mostly means most but not all of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: eaten, as in eaten away, means corroded

explanation.surface: Snagging a feather pen that is half wrecked and eaten away.
explanation.walkthrough: Rearrange A QUILL as ILLAQU, then add EATE: corroded is EATEN, and the second 'mostly' drops its N. The two matching 'mostly' phrases are Azed's balance; only the second removes a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Illaqueate is a rare Latinate verb, from laqueus, a noose, meaning to snare or ensnare.

clue.text: Tutor shortened Caribbean ballad

indicators.note: something shortened has lost its end, so the last letter is cut off

parts.note: a mentor is a tutor or guide

explanation.surface: A teacher cuts short a song from the Caribbean.
explanation.walkthrough: MENTOR drops its final R.
explanation.definitionFit: Mento is a Jamaican folk-song style, forerunner of ska and reggae, with topical ballad-like lyrics.

clue.text: Lady, not one poorly inside, in pond

indicators.note: inside means placed within, so one piece goes into the other
not means without, so the following item is taken away

parts.note: madam is a form of address for a lady

explanation.surface: A lady, who is not the one feeling unwell, is found in a pond.
explanation.walkthrough: Not one means one A leaves the lady, and the illness then goes in straight after her first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A milldam is the water held back by a dam to drive a mill wheel, a pond formed for that purpose.

clue.text: One aunt, uncommon, I'll follow, as the case indicates (10, three words)

indicators.note: uncommon means out of the ordinary, so the letters of the word before it appear in an unusual order

explanation.surface: An unusual aunt says she will follow on, as circumstances dictate.
explanation.walkthrough: Uncommon seems to do double duty, giving its synonym and also signalling that those letters are mixed with the aunt. The answer is a Latin tag, so the letters look strange until split into words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase a natura rei means 'from the nature of the thing', that is, as the circumstances themselves show.

clue.text: Mineral, 3-pin plugged

indicators.note: plugged here means wired up in a new way, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the numeral written as a word

explanation.surface: A mineral is wired into a three-pin plug.
explanation.walkthrough: The 3 looks like a reference to clue 3, but it is just the word three spelt out.
explanation.definitionFit: Prehnite is a pale green calcium aluminium silicate mineral, named after the Dutch colonel Hendrik von Prehn.

clue.text: Large vessel going round sea (not river), immense tract

indicators.note: going round means encircling, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: a vat is a large tank or tub

indicators.note: not means without, so the following word is taken away

parts.note: ea is a dialect word for a river

explanation.surface: A huge ship sails round the sea instead of the river, covering a vast expanse.
explanation.walkthrough: Ea, a river in Chambers, comes out of sea to leave S. Vast is used here as a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun, vast is a poetic word for a boundless expanse, as in 'the vast of heaven'.

clue.text: Hellebore plant HM placed in vessel, unusual

indicators.note: placed in means put inside, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: a vat is a large vessel

explanation.surface: The monarch puts an odd poisonous plant into a pot.
explanation.walkthrough: HM, Her Majesty, is ER in crosswords; rum is British slang for strange.
explanation.definitionFit: Veratrum is the genus of false hellebores, poisonous lilies once used medicinally.

clue.text: Grig found in lock, bare maybe

indicators.note: found in means located inside, so one piece sits within the other

parts.note: a tress is a lock of hair
a grig is a small eel

explanation.surface: A cricket turns up in a lock of hair, perhaps a bald one.
explanation.walkthrough: Grig means both a cricket and a small eel; the eel sense is wanted. Maybe flags that bare is only one example of the answer, as of a landscape.
explanation.definitionFit: A treeless landscape is bare of woodland, so bare describes it in one particular sense.

clue.text: Hat and bra disposed of in large country

indicators.note: disposed means arranged, so these letters are set out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written; and is a joiner

explanation.surface: Someone throws away a hat and a bra somewhere in a big country.
explanation.walkthrough: Disposed of reads as thrown away, but disposed means arranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Bharat is the official Hindi name of India, the world's most populous country.

clue.text: Gal, a bint with fringe dressed, cut square across

definitions.note: the answer is a noun, a tail cut square across

indicators.note: dressed hair is arranged afresh, so these letters are set in a new order

explanation.surface: A girl has her fringe styled and trimmed straight across.
explanation.walkthrough: With fringe hints at the answer, since a bang is a fringe; bint is British slang for a girl.
explanation.definitionFit: A bangtail is a horse's tail whose end is cut straight across, or a horse having such a tail.

clue.text: Writer involved in a diet, complicated — it consists of five ingredients

indicators.note: involved in means wrapped inside, so one piece goes within the other
something complicated is tangled, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A writer gets caught up in a complicated diet with five ingredients.
explanation.walkthrough: Pen as writer is a crossword staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Diapente is an old pharmacy term for a medicinal compound made from five ingredients, from Greek for 'through five'.

clue.text: Wind that's partly southern or thermal

indicators.note: partly says only a part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

parts.note: the letters run across the three words

explanation.surface: A breeze described as partly southern or a rising thermal.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface points to southern and thermal winds, but the answer is a north wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A norther is a strong cold wind from the north, especially one sweeping over Texas and the Gulf of Mexico.

clue.text: Recurrent refrain — see second note before favourite finish

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale

explanation.surface: A recurring chorus, a note that comes before the favourite's finishing line.
explanation.walkthrough: See works as a pointer, telling the solver to look at the wordplay that follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A repetend is a recurring word, phrase or refrain in poetry or music, also the repeating digits of a decimal.

clue.text: Strike alerts Russian workers' guilds

indicators.note: a strike knocks things about, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A strike sends warnings to Russian labour unions.
explanation.walkthrough: Strike reads as a labour stoppage, fitting the unions, but it is the signal to mix the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An artel was a cooperative association of workers or craftsmen in Russia, sharing work and profits.

clue.text: Woollen material I included in circular caps

indicators.note: included in means placed inside, so one piece goes within the other

explanation.surface: Woollen fabric that I have included in some round caps.
explanation.walkthrough: A tam is a Scottish bonnet, round and flat-topped.
explanation.definitionFit: Tamis is a fine woollen cloth used for straining, the same as tammy.

clue.text: Meat maybe about noon, dark red in colour

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: veal is an example of meat

explanation.surface: Some meat cooked around midday turns a dark red colour.
explanation.walkthrough: Venal here is the rare sense relating to veins, not the usual one meaning bribable.
explanation.definitionFit: In this rare sense, venal means venous, and blood in the veins is a deep dark red.

clue.text: Sins? Regular features in terrorism

indicators.note: regular features are letters taken at even intervals, every other one

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Wrongdoing is a regular part of terrorism.
explanation.walkthrough: Sins is a noun in the surface but stands for the verb, so the question mark admits the stretch.
explanation.definitionFit: To err is to go astray morally, so a verb meaning does wrong fits sins used as a verb.

clue.text: A bit of a kip, diffident, I've abandoned? Unsuccessful criminal effort

indicators.note: abandoned means left behind, so these letters are dropped from the word before

parts.note: the at is a Laotian coin, a hundredth of the kip

explanation.surface: A bit of a nap, a timid sleeper gives up; it was a botched crime.
explanation.walkthrough: Kip looks like British slang for a nap, but it is the currency of Laos.
explanation.definitionFit: An attentat is an attempted crime, especially a failed assassination attempt on a political figure.

clue.text: Gradual decline, first to last, again

indicators.note: first to last says the opening letter moves round to the end

parts.note: to be on the wane is to be in gradual decline

explanation.surface: Things slowly decline from first place to last, all over again.
explanation.definitionFit: Anew means once more, afresh, in a new way, which is what again says.

clue.text: Fish for eel down under — it's prickly

definitions.meaning: first meaning: in New Zealand the Maori word ... means an eel
second meaning: the prickly pear cactus

explanation.walkthrough: The obvious fish is a red herring: both senses are the antipodean eel and the cactus, not the tuna fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Tuna is a New Zealand name for the freshwater eel, and also a name for the prickly pear cactus or its fruit.

clue.text: Ferny scales chaps cut into NZ tree

indicators.note: cut into means set within, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: the rata is a New Zealand tree with crimson flowers

explanation.surface: Some men chop into a New Zealand tree whose bark has fern-like scales.
explanation.definitionFit: Ramenta are thin brownish scales found on the stems and leaves of many ferns.

clue.text: Style of jacket, male, kept in vessel coming back

indicators.note: coming back means returning, so the letters are read from the end
kept in means held inside, so one piece sits within the other

explanation.surface: A man's jacket is stored in a container on the return trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The male goes in after the second letter of the vessel, and the whole is then reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nehru jacket is a long hip-length coat with a mandarin collar, named after India's first prime minister.

clue.text: Urinates, ie messily, in a row

indicators.note: messily means in a disorderly way, so these letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone relieves themselves untidily while lined up in a queue.
explanation.definitionFit: Uniseriate is a botanical term for structures arranged in a single series or line.

clue.text: Foreign sparrow that is lost in boggy ground

indicators.note: lost means gone missing, so the letters for that is drop out

parts.note: the mossie is the Cape sparrow of South Africa
ie, id est, means that is

explanation.surface: A bird from abroad goes missing in a swamp.
explanation.walkthrough: Moss in the Scottish and northern sense is a peat bog.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scotland and northern England a moss is a bog or tract of wet peaty land.

clue.text: Plant genus completely surrounded by a wire twisted

indicators.note: surrounded by means enclosed, so one piece sits inside the other
twisted means bent out of shape, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A plant is wrapped all round in some bent wire.
explanation.definitionFit: Walleria is a genus of African and Australian tuberous plants in the lily family.
